chapter_theme: The great battle with the Vidyadharas: they are shamed back into the fight, Sri Sena and Sripala join it, a fall of the Vidyadhara king's crown breaks his army, and Kanaka Chitran taunts the kings who flee from fated men.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara warriors and kings of the mountain, one side of the battle
the bright-spear Vidyadhara leader who rallies the men
the Vidyadhara king whose crown falls
a warrior of good conduct who enters the fight like Death
the hero who joins the fight and mounts the horse
son of the discus-holder, who steps in when the kings break

1357.reading: A voice taunts the men who run, saying that flight to save a body costs the jewel of honour, and that a forest awaits those who fear.
1357.nuance: The second half (lines 3-4) is obscure and the speaker is not named; the reading holds only line 1-2 firmly, and 1358 suggests the words are a rally to men who had begun to flee.
1357.event: A speaker shames the fleeing Vidyadharas for abandoning honour to save their lives.

claims.claim: a warrior who flees to save his life throws away his honour

1358.reading: At these words the Vidyadharas turn back and take up the fight, and the bright-spear leader urges them on.
1358.event: The Vidyadharas rally and return to the battle at their leader's urging.

1359.reading: The sword-bearing Vidyadharas crowd in against the enemy and the warriors are cut to pieces at the neck and the body.
1359.event: Vidyadharas and the enemy's swordsmen close and cut each other down.

1360.reading: Pieces of horses, saddle-gear and cut flanks lie mixed over the whole battlefield.

1361.reading: Sparks fly from the clashing swords like fire, and tusked elephants fall like mountains.

1362.reading: Men sink into mud made of gore, the tracks of the field fill with blood, and the fronts of golden chariots are broken.
1362.nuance: Word division is broken in lines 1-3; the picture of the chariot-front shattered in blood is firm, the rest is held loosely.

1363.reading: Sri Sena, a man of good conduct, comes into the sword fight like Death himself.

1364.reading: A boast that the speaker can fight those who live on earth and those who live in the sky alike.
1364.nuance: No line names the speaker; I take it as Sri Sena because 1363 has just introduced him, and the sky-dwellers are the flying Vidyadharas.
1364.event: A fighter boasts of fighting both earthly and sky-dwelling foes.

1365.reading: Hearing the angry challenge to take up weapons if they can fight this kind of war, Sripala comes in.
1365.event: Sripala, hearing the challenge, joins the fight.

1366.reading: The chief mounts a horse decked with whisks that rises like a wave of the sea, and frightens everyone.
1366.event: The hero mounts his horse and terrifies the enemy.

1367.reading: Horses wheel and rise in their circling and the bow-and-arrow kings are bewildered in the fight.
1367.event: The horses wheel and the opposing kings lose their order.

1368.reading: Bow, sword and spear are laid aside as if by a word, and the combatants begin a fight without limit.
1368.event: The fighters give up weapons and begin close combat.

1369.reading: The victorious Vidyadhara, broad-chested, breaks the other's bow and hurled spear with ease.
1369.event: The Vidyadhara breaks his opponent's bow and spear.

1370.reading: With his spear broken the enemy cuts it down and strikes with a victorious sword at the king.
1370.nuance: The word division is very broken and who strikes whom cannot be fixed.
1370.event: A sword stroke is aimed at the king.

1371.reading: The sword strikes a shining shoulder and the wounded man stretches himself out.

1372.reading: A wound made by the sword is said to be washed bright and clear in a garlanded man's honey-smelling flowers.
1372.nuance: The verse is built on rhyming forms in -ளித and is very hard to parse; the reading is a guess at its main sense.

1373.reading: After the laid-on sword has cut, the garlanded man urges his unruly horse not to go on.
1373.event: A rider drives his horse away from the fight.

1374.reading: He who let his horse run over the swift mount thinks of harming the other's shining crown.
1374.event: A rider plans to strike at the enemy's crown.

1375.reading: He thinks of cutting the crown, and the leap that follows is greater than any on earth or in the sky.
1375.event: The rider leaps up to strike the crown.

1376.reading: At the sign of his own sword he flies up on his course, through the sky, and reaches the world's edge.
1376.event: The rider flies up through the sky.

1377.reading: The great gem-crown of the flying Vidyadhara falls like a star at the other king's weapon.
1377.event: The Vidyadhara king's crown is struck down by his rival.

1378.reading: As the lord's bright crown falls, the mountain-folk's army gives up the fight and turns its back.
1378.nuance: The verse shows that an army stands or falls with its king's crown; it is the narrator's picture, not a stated rule.
1378.event: The Vidyadhara army breaks and flees when the crown falls.

1379.reading: As the mountain kings break, Kanaka Chitran, the discus-holder's son, angry at heart, steps in and speaks.
1379.event: Kanaka Chitran enters the fight and speaks.

1380.reading: A speaker says that a man with drawn sword and girded belt who runs in fear of one man shows a manliness that is to be despised.
1380.nuance: 1379 says Kanaka Chitran spoke; I take this as his speech, but the verse itself names nobody.
1380.event: Kanaka Chitran taunts the fleeing kings for their cowardice.

claims.claim: a man with a sword in hand who flees from one man has a loathsome manliness

1381.reading: The Vidyadharas of the high mountain turn back in fear of men whom fate has marked, and the fanged youth laughs in wonder.
1381.nuance: விதிபடு is read as 'fate-marked'; the identity of the laughing youth is not named and may be Kanaka Chitran or Sripala.
1381.event: The Vidyadhara kings retreat; a fanged young man laughs at the marvel.

claims.claim: men whom fate favours cannot be faced even by the strong Vidyadharas

links.note: 1357 shames men who run to save life; 1380 calls a swordsman who runs from one man loathsome.
links.teaches: The rally and the taunt are one argument in two voices: flight is judged first as lost honour, then as disgusting manhood.

links.note: 1366 shows the hero mounted and frightening all; 1381 shows the enemy kings turning back in fear.
links.teaches: The terror one rider causes at the start is what finally sends the whole Vidyadhara line home.

links.note: The falling crown of 1377 is followed at once by the army's flight in 1378.
links.teaches: The crown's fall is shown as the cause of the rout, not merely its sign.

links.note: 1378 shows an army breaking at the sight of its king's fallen crown; the Kural says an army needs leaders.
links.teaches: A fallen crown scatters an army that Kural 770 would call leaderless, showing the leader's role as a matter of sight as much as of command.

gains.a: The rout gains a general rule: the army broke because it had no head to keep it together.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene in which the leader's loss is not death but a crown struck off, and the effect is instant.

links.note: 1380 calls flight from one man loathsome; Kural 775 says even a blink at a hurled spear is flight.
links.teaches: The two texts set the line of disgrace at different places: the epic at running away, the Kural already at the flinch.

gains.a: The taunt gains a stricter test: by Kural 775 the Vidyadharas' shame began before they turned.
gains.b: The couplet gains a speaker who shames living men in front of their army, not a rule stated apart.

links.note: 1380 condemns a fleeing swordsman; Purananuru 278 gives a mother's vow to cut her breast when told her son fled.
links.teaches: The Sangam poem shows what the epic's taunt costs the one who runs: the family's shame, not only his own.

gains.a: The taunt gains a household that would mourn and punish the runaway.
gains.b: The Sangam poem gains a Jain-epic scene where the same charge of fleeing is thrown at kings in the middle of a battle.

links.note: 1381 says the mountain Vidyadharas fled from men whom fate has marked; Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate.
links.teaches: The epic gives fate as the one reason a strong flying army can be turned by men with no such powers.

gains.a: The Vidyadhara retreat gains a cause beyond skill or number: the opponents are fated to win.
gains.b: The couplet gains a battlefield instance in which fate beats a stronger force without any scheme being named.

source_issues: Verses 1362, 1370-1377 have broken word division and several readings are held loosely.
Verse 1376 has a stray full stop at the end of line 3.
Who fights whom in 1369-1377 cannot be fixed from the Tamil alone.
